Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Buyer-side assessment

The “STANDARD”, “FINAL” and “settled” labels are the Seller’s characterisations, not a reason to accept these terms. The documents themselves disclose unresolved risks and inconsistencies. The positions should be tested against Wattlebridge’s bargain: acquire 100% of Paperbark Analytics for AUD 24 million on a debt-free, cash-free basis, with meaningful recourse if the business or its assets are not as represented.

The full SPA and due diligence materials are not included here, so this is a review of the Seller’s stated positions and disclosure letter—not a clause-by-clause opinion on the complete agreement.

## Priority pushbacks

1. **Riverlark debt and security: resolve at Completion, not after it.**  
   The facility has approximately AUD 3.2 million outstanding, and the disclosure says it has not been repaid and no final security discharge is in the data room. A promise to provide a release after Completion leaves the Buyer exposed to debt and encumbered assets after it has paid the price. Require repayment from the Completion funds flow, delivery of lender payout and release documents (or a tightly controlled escrow/undertaking mechanism), and confirmation that all security is discharged. The price mechanics should expressly deduct debt and other debt-like items and deal with cash and transaction expenses consistently with the debt-free, cash-free basis.

2. **Bluefen: make effective consent a Completion condition.**  
   Bluefen represents about AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue. The disclosure identifies a change-of-control clause and conditions, but contains neither final written consent nor evidence those conditions are met. “Reasonable endeavours” is not enough for a customer of this significance, and consent should not be deemed satisfied merely by delivery of a document if its conditions remain outstanding. Require valid, unconditional (or Buyer-approved) written consent and satisfaction of the relevant conditions before Completion, with a termination right if not obtained. Consider whether a price, indemnity or other remedy is needed if the consent is not obtained or the customer terminates.

3. **Completion bonuses: reconcile the AUD 420,000 before signing or Completion.**  
   DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses that are absent from the draft funds flow. That is a material mismatch with the price mechanics, not merely a matter between Seller and employees. Establish the full cost, including any payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs; identify who is liable; and ensure the amount is not funded by the Buyer or left as a Company liability contrary to the agreed economics. Address it expressly in the funds flow and any debt-like items, leakage covenant, or specific indemnity. Confirm whether the bonuses are earned, payable at Completion, and conditional on continued employment.

4. **Ironquay: the current indemnity may not secure the IP the Buyer expects to acquire.**  
   Under DD-004, transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee; DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open, with no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment in the room. The Seller’s assertion that an existing indemnity is “adequate” does not establish that Paperbark owns or can transfer the materials. Require verified payment and a signed, effective assignment (including any necessary consents and moral-rights consents) before Completion. If that cannot be achieved, require an adequate escrow/retention and specific indemnity covering loss of use, replacement or remediation costs, third-party claims and related losses—not just the SOW3 payment.

5. **Export/privacy incident: investigate and allocate risk expressly.**  
   DD-006 describes a download link sent to an unintended external address and potentially about 1,240 records, while access, scope and notification obligations remain unknown. It is not established as a confirmed breach, but that uncertainty is precisely why it should not be dismissed as preliminary or immaterial. Require prompt completion of the investigation, preservation of evidence, appropriate notifications and remediation, and delivery of the findings. Obtain specific warranties and, depending on diligence findings, a tailored indemnity for pre-Completion privacy incidents, regulatory response, remediation and third-party claims. Avoid language that deems the matter accepted merely because it was disclosed.

## Liability, disclosure and recourse

- **General cap of AUD 4.8 million (20% of price):** This may leave the Buyer underprotected, particularly for a SaaS business where customer, data, IP and operational issues can be material. Push for a higher general cap, supported by the risk profile and diligence, and ensure the cap is not shared with separate specific indemnities. Fundamental matters—at least title, capacity and authority—should have a separate, substantially higher cap (often up to the purchase price or the relevant proceeds), rather than the general-warranty cap. Tax and IP may also warrant separate treatment.

- **AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 deductible basket:** The basket is about 1.04% of price, and the proposal makes only the excess recoverable. Push for a lower basket and a tipping basket (once the threshold is crossed, recovery from the first dollar), or at minimum a lower deductible. Clarify aggregation of related claims and that the de minimis does not exclude a series of related losses. Neither threshold should apply to fraud, deliberate concealment, fundamental claims or specific indemnities.

- **18-month general warranty period:** Push for a longer period, particularly for tax, title, authority and claims that may take time to emerge. Tax claims should run at least through the applicable statutory assessment period plus a buffer; fundamental claims should have a longer period or run to the relevant limitation period. A claim properly notified before expiry should survive until resolved, and the notice standard should not require a fully quantified claim before the facts are known.

- **Applying all limitations to every claim:** Reject the proposed default. Limitations, caps, baskets, time bars, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions should not automatically apply to fraud, deliberate concealment, title/fundamental claims, specific indemnities, debt or funds-flow obligations, or claims under covenants and Completion undertakings. Specify the treatment of each category expressly.

- **Buyer-knowledge bar:** Reject a bar for matters known by the Buyer or its advisers, including matters discoverable in diligence. It creates disputes about whose knowledge counts and rewards incomplete disclosure. At most, negotiate a narrowly defined, actual-knowledge standard for specifically identified individuals, with no imputation from data-room access or constructive knowledge. Knowledge should not bar claims for fraud, deliberate concealment, fundamental matters or specific indemnities.

- **General disclosure of the entire data room and public records:** Reject blanket incorporation of DD-002 to DD-012 and public records as sufficient disclosure against warranties. It risks converting a large, poorly targeted information set into a broad warranty carve-out. Require specific, fair disclosure against the particular warranty, with enough detail to identify the nature and reasonably foreseeable scope of the issue. Schedule 7 should not deem every data-room item disclosed merely because it was accessible. The reservation in paragraph 11 correctly says the Buyer must assess the facts, but it does not cure the breadth of paragraph 1.1.

## Other disclosed matters to address

- **Supplier renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate):** The documents do not establish whether the renewals are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. Review the contracts and commitments; confirm amounts and timing, whether they are accrued or payable, and whether any are debt-like or outside the ordinary course. Do not accept the Seller’s “ordinary-course operating costs” label as a substitute for that analysis.
- **Title:** DD-012 records Harbourglass as registered holder, but a register alone is not a complete warranty package. Require warranties covering good title, full legal and beneficial ownership, valid issue and fully paid shares, no encumbrances or third-party rights, and authority to transfer. Verify the register and corporate records independently and make title a Completion deliverable.
- **Tax and IP warranties:** The Seller’s statement that these are “settled” is not a substantive answer. Seek appropriate, specific warranties and separate limitation treatment where the risk warrants it, including ownership, chain of title, licences, infringement, open-source use and employee/contractor assignments, and tax returns, liabilities and audits.
- **Office lease and Mossvale:** The disclosure says neither provision establishes consent is required merely because shares are sold. Confirm the actual contractual position and any notice or consent requirements before Completion; do not infer from the disclosure that no action is needed. Include any required notices or consents as deliverables or conditions.

## Recommended negotiating position

Treat the Seller’s package as a starting draft, not an agreed bargain. First require Completion protections for Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment and security release, the bonuses and funds flow, and Ironquay ownership/assignment. Then revise the liability regime: improve the cap and basket, extend claim periods, separate fundamental/tax/IP and specific claims from the general regime, and remove blanket knowledge and disclosure defences. Finally, close the privacy, supplier, title, tax and IP diligence gaps and reflect any unresolved risk in targeted indemnities, price mechanics, escrow or a Completion condition.

Have NSW-qualified transaction counsel check the complete SPA, schedules, funds flow and underlying contracts before agreeing final drafting.
